Cell-Cell Communication — Method, Real Results & a Computed Comparison

A detailed look at scripts/06_export_for_cellchat.py + 07_cellchat_analysis.R: what CellChat infers, the real results on the full-scale annotated dataset, and a direct computed comparison against a naive (non-permutation-tested) baseline — quantifying exactly what the permutation test buys over just ranking by raw communication-probability magnitude.

907,696 → 694,803 cells 10 cell types 291 interactions / 19 pathways Real full-scale run, 2026-08-02
Method Results on real data Computed comparison Why they differ Caveats References

Method

What CellChat is actually inferring

CellChat1 infers likely cell-cell signaling from expression data alone — there is no direct physical measurement of communication in scRNA-seq, so every "interaction" below is a statistical inference, not an observation. For each curated ligand-receptor pair in its database (including multi-subunit receptor complexes, e.g. TGFBR1+TGFBR2) and each ordered pair of annotated cell types (source → target, including a type signaling to itself), CellChat computes a communication probability from the average expression of the ligand in the source group and the receptor in the target group, then tests whether that probability is higher than expected by chance via label permutation: cell-group labels are randomly reshuffled many times, the same probability is recomputed each time, and the real value is compared against that null distribution to get a p-value.

This pipeline feeds CellChat the output of 04b_better_annotation.py (confidence-gated cell-type labels), exporting only cells with a confident label — cells 04b flagged Ambiguous are excluded before CellChat ever sees them (--exclude-ambiguous), since feeding an uncertain label into a communication test would just launder that uncertainty into a false-looking signal.

Results

Results on the real full-scale dataset

Input: 907,696 QC-passed cells (from the real ~987,585-cell Parse dataset) → Harmony-integrated → clustered → annotated by 04b. 212,893 cells flagged Ambiguous were excluded, leaving 694,803 confidently-annotated cells across 10 cell types for CellChat.

CellChat found 291 significant ligand-receptor interactions across 19 signaling pathways (permutation p<0.05). Runtime was ~1.5 hours, almost entirely in the permutation step (computeCommunProb) — by far the slowest stage in the whole pipeline at this cell count.

Myeloid populations (cDC, pDC, both monocyte subsets) are both the most frequent senders and receivers by a wide margin — consistent with antigen-presenting cells being the hub of PBMC-scale intercellular signaling, and with cDC↔pDC being the single most cross-talking pair in the whole network (15 interactions cDC→pDC, 10 pDC→cDC).

Real computed comparison

Permutation testing vs. a naive probability-only baseline

CellChat's defining methodological choice is the permutation test — but is it actually necessary, or would just ranking every tested pair by raw communication probability and taking the top N get you basically the same answer? This is directly checkable from data CellChat already computed: cellchat@net$prob holds the communication probability for every tested (source, target, ligand-receptor pair) combination — not just the ones that passed the significance filter — and cellchat@net$pval holds the matching permutation p-value for each. No re-implementation of CellChat's internal expression/complex-handling logic was needed; both comparison arms come directly from the same already-computed object.

Naive baseline: take the same number of top hits (291) ranked purely by prob magnitude, with no significance test at all — "what if we'd just thresholded on probability and skipped the permutation step?"

QuantityCount
Total tested (source, target, L-R pair) combinations with prob > 0315
CellChat permutation-significant (p < 0.05)291
Naive top-291 by raw probability ∩ permutation-significant267 (91.8%)
Naive-only: high raw probability, but permutation-rejected24
Significant-only: permutation-significant, but ranked outside naive top-29124

The two methods mostly agree

91.8% overlap is substantial — most of what CellChat reports, a naive probability ranking would also have surfaced. The permutation test isn't reversing the naive answer; it's correcting the edges of it. That's a meaningfully different claim than "the naive method is useless," and the report should say exactly that, not overstate the permutation test's necessity.

The two 24-pair discrepancy sets are where the permutation test actually earns its cost:

  • 24 naive-only pairs had high raw probability but were not statistically distinguishable from a random relabeling of cell identities. 13 of these 24 involve the same ligand-receptor pair, CD55_ADGRE5, paired with T-cell/NK/Treg/pDC/Plasma-cell source-target combinations that got permutation p-values of exactly 1 — i.e. indistinguishable from chance despite a nontrivial raw score. See the table below for the concrete examples.
  • 24 significant-only pairs were confirmed real by the permutation test despite not ranking in the naive top 291 by raw magnitude — cases where a modest-looking probability was still reliably non-random, likely reflecting a larger or lower-variance source/target group where even a smaller effect is statistically stable.

Probability magnitude is correlated with significance, but not a clean proxy for it

GroupMedian probability
Permutation-significant pairs0.0203
Non-significant pairs0.00757

Significant pairs have a ~2.7× higher median probability than non-significant ones (Wilcoxon rank-sum, W=5291, p=2.7×10-5) — a real, statistically confirmed relationship. But it's a tendency, not a hard rule, which is exactly why the naive top-N approach mislabels 48 out of 315 tested pairs (24 each direction) relative to the permutation test.

Interpretation

Why the two methods diverge where they do

The permutation test isn't just a magnitude threshold in disguise — it's implicitly correcting for group size and expression variance, which raw probability doesn't see at all. A cell-type pair with few cells (e.g. pDC and Plasma cell are the two smallest annotated groups here, 4,207 and 3,387 cells respectively out of 694,803) can produce a deceptively confident-looking raw probability from a handful of high-expressing cells, while the same magnitude in a much larger, noisier group is a much weaker signal relative to what random relabeling would produce by chance. That's precisely the failure mode the 13 CD55_ADGRE5 naive-only false positives above show: plausible-looking raw scores involving several of the smaller/rarer cell types in this dataset, all rejected outright (p=1) by the permutation test.

The reverse direction — 24 pairs the permutation test confirmed despite a modest raw score — is the flip side of the same mechanism: a large, low-variance group can make even a modest true effect statistically distinguishable from noise, where a fixed magnitude threshold alone would have discarded it.

Caveats

What this result does and doesn't show

  • Inference, not observation. Every number above comes from co-expression statistics, not a direct measurement of signaling. Treat strong hits as hypotheses to validate (literature, targeted follow-up), not confirmed biology.
  • No sample/donor structure passed to CellChat. The export step doesn't currently carry the donor (sample) column into CellChat's metadata — CellChat itself warned "The 'meta' data does not have a column named samples... all cells are assumed to belong to sample1". This run treats all 24 donors as one pooled population for the communication test; it cannot currently detect donor-specific signaling differences. Worth revisiting if a donor-level comparison (e.g. healthy vs. T1D) becomes the actual question.
  • Ambiguous cells are excluded, not resolved. The 212,893 cells 04b couldn't confidently label are simply absent from this analysis — real signaling involving those cells (whatever they are) isn't represented here at all.
  • Database coverage is finite. CellChat's curated ligand-receptor database won't contain every real pathway — a pathway of biological interest that's absent from these results may reflect database coverage, not biological absence. See docs/pipeline_overview.html's reference to broader database surveys2 if a specific pathway is expected but missing.
  • Single time point. This is a static snapshot — it says which interactions are statistically supported in this data, not how they change over time or in response to perturbation.
